title: Judas Didn't Betray Jesus Because of Money
paragraphs:
Judas Didn't Betray Jesus Because of Money
The Scandal Nobody Talks About: The Real Reason Judas Walked Away From the Son of God
What if one of the most repeated assumptions in Christian history is only telling part of the story?
What if Judas Iscariot did not ultimately betray Jesus because he loved money?
What if the silver was only the symptom of something much deeper, darker, and far more relatable?
Because if we're honest, most people are not destroyed by what they worship.
They are destroyed by what they expected God to do that He didn't do.
And suddenly Judas becomes less like a villain from a stained-glass window and more like a mirror.
That is what makes this story terrifying.
And that is what makes the Gospel so beautiful.
The story begins with a man who had front-row seats to the greatest life ever lived.
Judas walked with Jesus.
He heard every sermon.
He witnessed blind eyes open.
He watched demons flee.
He saw storms obey a voice.
He carried responsibilities among the disciples.
John 12:6 reveals that Judas kept the money bag, indicating that he managed the group's finances.
Yet Scripture gradually pulls back the curtain on a tragedy unfolding inside his heart.
Many people point immediately to the thirty pieces of silver.
Matthew 26:14-15 says:
"Then one of the twelve, whose name was Judas Iscariot, went to the chief priests and said, 'What will you give me if I deliver him over to you?' And they paid him thirty pieces of silver."
The amount was real.
The betrayal was real.
The silver mattered.
But Scripture never says money was the deepest reason.
In fact, when we allow the whole biblical narrative to speak, something even more sobering emerges.
The Greek word used in Matthew 26 for betrayal is "παραδίδωμι" (paradidōmi), meaning "to hand over," "to deliver up," or "to surrender into another's hands."
Judas did not simply steal.
He delivered Jesus into the hands of those he knew wanted Him dead.
Why?
Because somewhere along the journey, Judas stopped following the real Jesus and started following a version of Jesus he had created in his own expectations.
Many Jews in the first century longed for a political Messiah.
They expected a king who would overthrow Rome.
A conqueror.
A revolutionary.
A national liberator.
Even some of Jesus' closest followers struggled with this expectation.
Again and again Jesus spoke of suffering, death, humility, and sacrifice.
Again and again the disciples struggled to understand.
The kingdom Jesus proclaimed looked nothing like the kingdom many wanted.
The prophet Isaiah had already described Him centuries earlier:
"He was despised and rejected by men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief." (Isaiah 53:3)
Yet many wanted a warrior.
Jesus came as a Savior.
Many wanted a throne.
Jesus carried a cross.
Many wanted vengeance.
Jesus preached forgiveness.
Many wanted power.
Jesus demonstrated surrender.
And that collision between expectation and reality has shattered countless hearts throughout history.
Not because Jesus failed.
Because He refused to become what people demanded.
Judas may have loved money.
Scripture certainly reveals greed in his character.
John records Judas objecting when Mary anointed Jesus with expensive perfume.
But John immediately exposes the motive:
"He said this, not because he cared about the poor, but because he was a thief." (John 12:6)
Greed was present.
But greed alone cannot fully explain what happened next.
People steal money every day.
Few betray the Son of God with a kiss.
Something deeper was growing.
Disillusionment.
Disappointment.
Unmet expectations.
The dangerous belief that Jesus was not becoming the Messiah Judas wanted Him to be.
The tragedy is that Judas stood closer to Jesus physically than almost anyone in history while simultaneously drifting farther away spiritually.
That should terrify every churchgoer.
Because proximity to Jesus is not the same thing as surrender to Jesus.
You can attend church and still miss Christ.
You can know Bible verses and still resist His lordship.
You can sing worship songs and still secretly demand that God serve your agenda.
The Hebrew heart of Scripture consistently warns against this danger.
The word לֵב (lev) means "heart," not merely emotions but the center of one's will, desires, thoughts, and loyalty.
God has always wanted the heart.
Not performances.
Not appearances.
Not religious activity.
The heart.
And Judas gradually gave his heart to something else.
Perhaps ambition.
Perhaps disappointment.
Perhaps control.
Perhaps a kingdom of his own making.
Whatever occupied that throne eventually pushed Jesus from it.
Then came the kiss.
The most heartbreaking symbol in the Gospel narrative.
Luke 22:48 records Jesus asking:
"Judas, would you betray the Son of Man with a kiss?"
A kiss.
An act normally reserved for affection.
An act of friendship.
An act of closeness.
The very symbol of love became the vehicle of betrayal.
That is the scandal.
Not merely that Judas sold Jesus.
But that he appeared close while his heart had already left.
Yet the deepest scandal is not Judas.
The deepest scandal is grace.
Because while Judas was betraying Jesus, Jesus was still moving toward the cross.
Still loving sinners.
Still fulfilling prophecy.
Still carrying the weight of humanity's rebellion.
Still choosing mercy.
The Greek word χάρις (charis) means grace—undeserved favor freely given.
And nowhere is grace more astonishing than at Calvary.
Because the cross was not God's emergency response to Judas' betrayal.
It was God's eternal plan to redeem a broken world.
Acts 2:23 declares that Jesus was delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God.
Judas was responsible for his choices.
Yet God remained sovereign.
Human evil could not derail divine redemption.
And that is where this story stops being about Judas and starts becoming about us.
Because most people have moments when God does not meet their expectations.
The prayer goes unanswered.
The healing doesn't come.
The relationship ends.
The diagnosis arrives.
The dream collapses.
The door closes.
And suddenly we face the same question Judas faced.
Will we follow Jesus for who He truly is?
Or only for who we hoped He would be?
Many abandon faith not because they studied too much.
Not because evidence disappeared.
Not because Christ failed.
But because Jesus refused to become the servant of their expectations.
The painful truth is that the Jesus who saves us is often not the Jesus we initially wanted.
He is better.
Holier.
Wiser.
More loving.
More faithful.
But He is also far less controllable.
And that is where true discipleship begins.
Not when Jesus follows our plans.
When we surrender to His.
The story of Judas is one of the greatest warnings in Scripture.
But the story of Jesus is one of the greatest invitations ever given.
Because every one of us has betrayed Him in some way.
Through pride.
Through rebellion.
Through selfishness.
Through unbelief.
Through hidden sin.
Yet Jesus still stretches out nail-scarred hands toward sinners.
Still offers forgiveness.
Still offers redemption.
Still offers a new beginning.
That is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
Not that humanity remained faithful.
But that Christ remained faithful when humanity failed.
Be honest.
This may have hit closer to home than you expected.
If you truly desire to glorify God through advancing the message of the Gospel, your support and sharing become part of that mission.
The most dangerous betrayal is not abandoning Jesus in anger—it is quietly replacing Him with the version of Him you wish existed.
